articles.content: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well. Continue reading...

articles.content: In trying to save for a house deposit, she had sacrificed activities that brought her joy. And constant checking of her bank balance exacerbated her fears The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work “It all feels so hard. It’s impossible to get ahead. It’s not even two steps forward and one step back, now it’s one step forward and two steps back.” Like many people, Claudia* was feeling the impact of the cost-of-living crisis. Despite professional qualifications and full-time employment, she felt increasing financial insecurity and a lack of confidence about future opportunities. Claudia lamented her chance of fulfilling her long-held dream of buying a home. Meanwhile, her peers who had already entered the property market were feeling the pinch due to work insecurity, interest rate hikes and falling property prices. Continue reading...

articles.author: Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz
articles.content: Randomised trials of omega-6s do not show an increase in inflammation caused by the fatty acid Read more in the Antiviral series If you’ve been online lately, you’ve probably been bombarded with the discourse about seed oils. Once a completely innocuous food that no one really talked about, they have become the enemy of the moment. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of health and human services in the US, has called them “toxic” and vowed to act against them. There are countless activewear-clad influencers online saying that nothing harms your health more than these products. Which is odd, because the Australian dietary guidelines say seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines and most experts – why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.” Continue reading...

Which is odd, because the Australian dietary guidelines say seed oils are basically fine. You should limit them because they’re high in calories but otherwise there’s no major reason – according to the guidelines and most experts – why you should avoid them. As Prof Lauren Ball, director of the University of Queensland’s Centre for Community Health and Wellbeing, says: “There’s no convincing evidence that eating seed oils like canola or sunflower oil in normal dietary amounts harms our health. In fact, these oils contain unsaturated fats, which are generally beneficial for cardiovascular health.” Dr Jason Wu, a professor at the University of New South Wales, agrees: “The evidence base consistently points to health benefits of eating seed oils.” Continue reading...
articles.title: Are seed oils unhealthy? Why are so many influencers speaking out against them? | Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz

articles.content: After more than a decade of global consultation, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) – a condition that affects one in eight women – has a new name. The hormonal disorder, estimated to affect 170 million women worldwide, will now be known as polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). The new name was spearheaded by the endocrinologist Prof Helena Teede, the director of Melbourne’s Monash Centre for Health Research and Implementation. For too long, experts say, the misleading nature of the term 'polycystic' in PCOS contributed to delayed diagnosis and inadequate medical care. articles.author: Peter Breadon
articles.content: With initial consults now costing hundreds of dollars, we must embrace a national plan to boost targeted training, cover gaps and curb excessive charges A referral to a specialist doctor can be scary; you might be worried about getting a new diagnosis or hearing that your condition has gotten worse. But many Australians have an additional worry: whether they can afford the fee. Fees have surged, and they’re not slowing down. They’ve risen by 78% since 2010 on top of inflation. An initial consultation now often costs hundreds of dollars. $1,000 for a one-hour appointment: why are fees for Australia’s specialist doctors skyrocketing? What are my rights when I need to see a specialist doctor – and what if I can’t afford the fee? Struggling to afford specialist doctors’ fees?
